```

It is a mention rather than a command. Here it becomes an ask, exactly as a viewer pressing a button does, and the table still accepts it: the run has to be taking asks, and the same rate holds as for anything else asking. A kind this end does not know is ignored, so a tool that says more than `died` does not break against an older server.

### The profile

Which operation a result means is a **control profile**, kept with the run and edited in the app, never in the pack. A pack that only worked with one program attached to one game would not be a pack, and every pack here still plays with nothing attached at all.

A profile is a setup set and a list of rows. A row selects by the entry a result landed on, by a tag the entry carries, or by a whole table, and says what to do, for how long, and who it reaches.

```json
{
  "tool": "TarnishedTool",
  "setup": [{ "op": "flag.set", "args": { "name": "player.noRoll", "value": true } }],
  "rows": [
    { "tag": "curse", "label": "A curse", "until": "unit",
      "ops": [{ "op": "speffect.apply", "args": { "id": 6900 } }] },
    { "entry": "rot", "table": "curse", "for": 90,
      "ops": [{ "op": "speffect.apply", "args": { "id": 6900 } }] },
    { "table": "relocate", "to": "all",
      "ops": [{ "op": "warp.position", "args": { "block": 60, "x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3 } }] }
  ]
}
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `tool` | The program this was written for, as that program names itself in its `hello`. Anything else listening is sent nothing and told why. Leave it out and the profile is for whatever is attached, which is how a script of your own works with no ceremony. |
| `setup` | Operations applied when a tool attaches, held for the run. The run's terms: the level, the restrictions, the things that would otherwise be a paragraph in a description and fifteen boxes ticked by hand. |
| `chosen` | On an operation in `setup`: it came from the loadout the run is played under rather than from the profile itself, and goes out under the id `loadout` instead of `setup`. Written by the run's own device when it publishes; a profile you write by hand has no use for it. |
| `table`, `entry`, `tag` | What a row matches. An entry, with its table where two tables share an id; a tag the entry carries, which is how one row covers a table full of curses; or a whole table. A row matching none of these is ignored rather than matching everything. |
| `label` | What a person sees in the tool's log. Without one, the line the table drew. |
| `for` | Seconds. |
| `until` | `unit`, for an effect that lasts the unit it landed in. Everything a unit applied comes off when that unit closes. Where a row somehow says both, the seconds win. |
| `to` | A seat's name, or `all`, or left out, which is also everyone. Matched against what a tool said it was sitting in front of, ignoring case. A tool that never said hears only what is for everyone. |
| `ops` | What to do, in order, as one thing. |

`to` names a seat, or `all`, or is left out, which is also everyone. A tool that never said which player it is hears only what is for everyone. Every matching row lands as its own effect, so a tag row covering eleven curses and an entry row for the twelfth both apply without either knowing about the other. A row selecting nothing at all is ignored rather than matching everything.

The operation names are the tool's, not ours. This end sends only what a profile names; that end refuses by name anything its build does not have, so a profile that gets ahead of somebody's version degrades instead of failing. Which also means a mapping somebody got wrong is fixed here, in the app, rather than in a program everyone has to download again.

Names are the compatibility story between versions of one program, and say nothing between programs: two tools for two games could easily both have a `warp.position`. That is what `tool` is for.

## Driving a run from a deck: `wss://…/ws?token=<jwt>&as=deck`

Everything above reads, or writes only through an ask. A deck presses the same buttons the page does: primary, a move, undo, an answer. It needs a signed-in account rather than a key — the app's own sign-in, the CLI's `runlog login`, or a client of its own that has been through the same WorkOS sign-in — and driving a run from a deck is part of Plus where plans are on. The token here is that account's access token, not a link's token or a stream key; those open the plain watcher and scene sockets described above, never a deck. The same address answers on the dev copy, at `wss://runlog.dev.scrthq.com`.

A deck names no run at connect: it is told what is open to it and picks. Only a run some other device is actively holding open ever appears, and pressing never reaches further than that.

### The runs it may press

A deck speaks first:

```json
{ "t": "hello" }
```

The answer, and again whenever the set changes, is the runs held open to this account on a writing device:

```json
{ "t": "runs", "runs": [{ "id": "01RUN", "name": "Thursday", "packTitle": "Forfeits", "held": true }] }
```

`name` and `packTitle` are left out where the run has none. A run that nothing is holding open drops off this list rather than being marked otherwise, so an empty `runs` reads as nothing open right now.

### Watching one

```json
{ "t": "watch", "id": "01RUN" }
```

From then on this run's `{ "t": "changed", "id": "01RUN", "seq": 42 }` rings on the same socket, exactly as it does for a watcher, and `seq` is what a press must carry.

### Pressing

```json
{ "t": "drive", "run": "01RUN", "seq": 42, "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "press": "primary" }
```

| `press` | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `primary` | The one button the page would show first: rolling a table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next one. |
| `move` | One of the run's moves, named by id in a `move` field. |
| `undo` | Takes back the last result, where there is one to take back. |
| `answer` | Answers what the run is asking for: `{ "subject": "Bowl 3" }` for a step that wants a name typed, or `{ "ticks": "all" }` for a step with a checklist, which ticks everything on it and presses the step's own finish button in the one press. |

`seq` names the offer a press was drawn from — the run's `events.length` at the moment it was shown — so a press made against last minute's state cannot land on whatever the run has moved on to since. `ref` is the caller's own; a press whose `ref` has been sent before on this connection settles to the same verdict rather than being taken twice.

### The verdict

```json
{ "t": "drove", "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "ok": true, "seq": 43 }
{ "t": "drove", "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "ok": false, "say": "That moved on." }
```

A verdict from the page carries `seq`, the run's own `events.length` once the press has landed: the `changed` that would otherwise carry it is a sync settle behind, and a deck pressing twice inside that window would name a `seq` the run had already moved past. Take it as you take the one on `changed`. The server's own refusals carry none, because nothing moved.

A verdict is the only answer a press gets, and a socket can drop one: treat a press with no verdict within a few seconds as lost, and press again with the same `ref`, which settles to the first verdict where the press did land.

It comes from the page holding the run wherever one is there to answer, since only that device knows what the press did. The server answers instead when there is nowhere for the press to go, or the press is not this account's to make:

    { "entry": "rot", "table": "curse", "for": 90,
      "ops": [{ "op": "speffect.apply", "args": { "id": 6900 } }] },
    { "table": "relocate", "to": "all",
      "ops": [{ "op": "warp.position", "args": { "block": 60, "x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3 } }] }
  ]
}
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `tool` | The program this was written for, as that program names itself in its `hello`. Anything else listening is sent nothing and told why. Leave it out and the profile is for whatever is attached, which is how a script of your own works with no ceremony. |
| `setup` | Operations applied when a tool attaches, held for the run. The run's terms: the level, the restrictions, the things that would otherwise be a paragraph in a description and fifteen boxes ticked by hand. |
| `chosen` | On an operation in `setup`: it came from the loadout the run is played under rather than from the profile itself, and goes out under the id `loadout` instead of `setup`. Written by the run's own device when it publishes; a profile you write by hand has no use for it. |
| `table`, `entry`, `tag` | What a row matches. An entry, with its table where two tables share an id; a tag the entry carries, which is how one row covers a table full of curses; or a whole table. A row matching none of these is ignored rather than matching everything. |
| `label` | What a person sees in the tool's log. Without one, the line the table drew. |
| `for` | Seconds. |
| `until` | `unit`, for an effect that lasts the unit it landed in. Everything a unit applied comes off when that unit closes. Where a row somehow says both, the seconds win. |
| `to` | A seat's name, or `all`, or left out, which is also everyone. Matched against what a tool said it was sitting in front of, ignoring case. A tool that never said hears only what is for everyone. |
| `ops` | What to do, in order, as one thing. |

`to` names a seat, or `all`, or is left out, which is also everyone. A tool that never said which player it is hears only what is for everyone. Every matching row lands as its own effect, so a tag row covering eleven curses and an entry row for the twelfth both apply without either knowing about the other. A row selecting nothing at all is ignored rather than matching everything.

The operation names are the tool's, not ours. This end sends only what a profile names; that end refuses by name anything its build does not have, so a profile that gets ahead of somebody's version degrades instead of failing. Which also means a mapping somebody got wrong is fixed here, in the app, rather than in a program everyone has to download again.

Names are the compatibility story between versions of one program, and say nothing between programs: two tools for two games could easily both have a `warp.position`. That is what `tool` is for.

## Driving a run from a deck: `wss://…/ws?token=<jwt>&as=deck`

Everything above reads, or writes only through an ask. A deck presses the same buttons the page does: primary, a move, undo, an answer. It needs a signed-in account rather than a key — the app's own sign-in, the CLI's `runlog login`, or a client of its own that has been through the same WorkOS sign-in — and driving a run from a deck is part of Plus where plans are on. The token here is that account's access token, not a link's token or a stream key; those open the plain watcher and scene sockets described above, never a deck. The same address answers on the dev copy, at `wss://runlog.dev.scrthq.com`.

A deck names no run at connect: it is told what is open to it and picks. Only a run some other device is actively holding open ever appears, and pressing never reaches further than that.

### The runs it may press

A deck speaks first:

```json
{ "t": "hello" }
```

The answer, and again whenever the set changes, is the runs held open to this account on a writing device:

```json
{ "t": "runs", "runs": [{ "id": "01RUN", "name": "Thursday", "packTitle": "Forfeits", "held": true }] }
```

`name` and `packTitle` are left out where the run has none. A run that nothing is holding open drops off this list rather than being marked otherwise, so an empty `runs` reads as nothing open right now.

### Watching one

```json
{ "t": "watch", "id": "01RUN" }
```

From then on this run's `{ "t": "changed", "id": "01RUN", "seq": 42 }` rings on the same socket, exactly as it does for a watcher, and `seq` is what a press must carry.

### Pressing

```json
{ "t": "drive", "run": "01RUN", "seq": 42, "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "press": "primary" }
```

| `press` | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `primary` | The one button the page would show first: rolling a table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next one. |
| `move` | One of the run's moves, named by id in a `move` field. |
| `undo` | Takes back the last result, where there is one to take back. |
| `answer` | Answers what the run is asking for: `{ "subject": "Bowl 3" }` for a step that wants a name typed, or `{ "ticks": "all" }` for a step with a checklist, which ticks everything on it and presses the step's own finish button in the one press. |

`seq` names the offer a press was drawn from — the run's `events.length` at the moment it was shown — so a press made against last minute's state cannot land on whatever the run has moved on to since. `ref` is the caller's own; a press whose `ref` has been sent before on this connection settles to the same verdict rather than being taken twice.

### The verdict

```json
{ "t": "drove", "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "ok": true, "seq": 43 }
{ "t": "drove", "ref": "cli-1758000000000", "ok": false, "say": "That moved on." }
```

A verdict from the page carries `seq`, the run's own `events.length` once the press has landed: the `changed` that would otherwise carry it is a sync settle behind, and a deck pressing twice inside that window would name a `seq` the run had already moved past. Take it as you take the one on `changed`. The server's own refusals carry none, because nothing moved.

A verdict is the only answer a press gets, and a socket can drop one: treat a press with no verdict within a few seconds as lost, and press again with the same `ref`, which settles to the first verdict where the press did land.

It comes from the page holding the run wherever one is there to answer, since only that device knows what the press did. The server answers instead when there is nowhere for the press to go, or the press is not this account's to make:

| `There is nothing to take back.` | The page; `undo` with nothing to undo. |
| `The run is not asking for that.` | The page; `answer` sent for a preset the current step does not have. |
| `That answer was empty.` | The page; a `subject` typed as nothing. |
| `This run does not know that press.` | The page; a `press` value that is none of the above. |
| `That press failed.` | The page; the press was on offer and got taken, and failed for a reason of its own with nothing to say about it. |

### What the page offers

The device holding the run publishes what a deck may press beside `control`, in its snapshot:

```json
{
  "offer": {
    "seq": 42,
    "primary": { "id": "roll", "label": "Draw the weather", "kind": "rollTable" },
    "moves": [{ "id": "died", "label": "Died" }],
    "undo": { "what": "A dry wind from the east." },
    "needsPage": null,
    "presets": []
  }
}
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `seq` | The offer's own `events.length`; the `seq` a press against it must carry. |
| `primary` | What a bare `primary` press takes: `id` is `roll`, `carry-on`, `close` or `enter`; `label` and `kind` are the step's own words. Null where nothing may be pressed without being asked something first. |
| `moves` | The moves a `move` press may name, by id and label. A move that would close the unit while something is still owed is left off rather than offered and refused. |
| `undo` | `{ "what": "…" }`, the last result in words, where there is one to take back; null otherwise. |
| `needsPage` | Why `primary` is null, in words a key face can show, such as "Draw the weather on the page"; null where nothing needs it. |
| `presets` | Steps that take a typed or ticked answer instead of a bare press: `{ "kind": "declareSubject", "label": "…", "suggestions": […] }`, answered with `{ "subject": "…" }`, `suggestions` left out where the run has none; or `{ "kind": "checklist", "label": "Tick everything and …", "items": 4 }`, answered with `{ "ticks": "all" }`. |

## Politeness

Poll no faster than every five seconds; the socket exists so you need not, and a widget is one reader on one machine, never one per viewer. Keep the token out of anything you publish: whoever has it can watch, and a widget pasted into a shared overlay carries it. If it gets out, **Stop sharing** and share again; the old token is dead the moment you do. Nothing here writes to the run except an ask, and an ask only asks.

## From the app

The widgets under **Stream** in the run's side column draw the same snapshot, on pages of their own, and **Everything, stacked** puts them in one column for a single browser source. See the guide's [Streaming a run](https://runlog.scrthq.com/guide/streaming) for those, and the pages after it for the apps.

      # releases and pushed tags alike. A release created by the App fires
      # the `release: published` event, and production picks it up.
      - name: Mint a token that can trigger the release event
        id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v3
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.CODE_MGR_APP_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.CODE_MGR_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}

      # The notes are the commit titles since the last tag, grouped by type
      # as cliff.toml says; the whole changelog, every release back to the
      # first, goes on the release as a file rather than into the tree, since
      # nothing but this job may write to main.
      - name: Write the release notes
        id: notes
        uses: orhun/git-cliff-action@v4
        with:
          config: cliff.toml
          args: --unreleased --tag ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }} --strip all
        env:
          OUTPUT: RELEASE_NOTES.md
      - name: Write the whole changelog
        uses: orhun/git-cliff-action@v4
        with:
          config: cliff.toml
          args: --tag ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}
        env:
          OUTPUT: CHANGELOG.md

      - name: Tag and publish
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          gh release create "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --target "${{ github.sha }}" \
            --title "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --notes-file RELEASE_NOTES.md \
            --latest \
            CHANGELOG.md

            echo ""
            if [ -n "${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}" ]; then echo "The number moved on the way: ${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}, because a release approved in between took the one dev was built with."; echo ""; fi

      # nothing but this job may write to main.
      - name: Write the release notes
        id: notes
        uses: orhun/git-cliff-action@v4
        with:
          config: cliff.toml
          args: --unreleased --tag ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }} --strip all
        env:
          OUTPUT: RELEASE_NOTES.md
      - name: Write the whole changelog
        uses: orhun/git-cliff-action@v4
        with:
          config: cliff.toml
          args: --tag ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}
        env:
          OUTPUT: CHANGELOG.md

      - name: Tag and publish
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          gh release create "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --target "${{ github.sha }}" \
            --title "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --notes-file RELEASE_NOTES.md \
            --latest \
            CHANGELOG.md

          {
            echo "### Released ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}"
            echo ""
            if [ -n "${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}" ]; then echo "The number moved on the way: ${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}, because a release approved in between took the one dev was built with."; echo ""; fi
            echo "Production deploys from the release event."
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

Release:
    name: Tag and publish
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    needs: DevDeploy
    environment: release
    permissions:
      contents: read
    concurrency:
      group: release
      cancel-in-progress: true
    steps:
      # Full history, for the tags and the notes since the last one.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      # The number the dev build was made with, and no other: a footer on
      # dev that says 0.0.140 is followed by a release called v0.0.140.
      - name: Take the version this build was made with
        id: release
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          next="${{ needs.DevDeploy.outputs.tag }}"
          if [ -z "$next" ]; then echo "::error::the deploy named no version"; exit 1; fi
          # Two builds waiting on a release both name the same next number;
          # once the older one is approved and tagged, the newer counts
          # again from the tag it made, since its commits include the
          # older's. The footer on dev said the old number for a while; the
          # release says the true one, and the summary says it moved.
          if git ls-remote --exit-code --tags origin "refs/tags/${next}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "${next} is tagged already: a release cut while this one waited took it. Counting again from the latest tag."
            git fetch --tags --quiet origin
            eval "$(bash .github/scripts/next-version.sh auto)"
            echo "moved=${next} -> ${tag}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            next="$tag"
          fi

# A Stream Deck at the table

Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and six actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Do the next thing, Press, Undo, and Metric. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.

## Signing in

Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.

**Sign in** shows a code and a link. Open the link in a browser, type the code, and you are signed in on the deck; the plugin keeps that sign-in in a file of its own, not in the settings the pages read. Signing in is not connecting: press Connect after.

## Connect

**Connect** opens the connection, and pressing it again closes it. Nothing is open until you press it, and a connection holding no run closes itself after thirty minutes — the key then says _Idle · press to connect_. A deck that is following a run stays up however long the stream goes.

Every other key says **Not connected**, with _press Connect_ beneath it, until the connection is open.

## The run the deck is on

The deck presses through the page that holds the run, so it only ever sees a run that is synced to your account and open on a page somewhere: the app in a browser tab, a [dock](#guide/dock), or a browser source. With nothing synced the keys say **Not synced**; with runs synced but none open, **No run open**.

**Run** names the run the deck is following. Press it to cycle through the runs open to you and pin the next one; its settings list the same runs by name. A pin holds: a pinned run that ends says **That run has ended** rather than moving the deck to whichever run went next. Where one run is open and nothing is pinned, the deck follows that one.

## The keys

- **Do the next thing** presses whatever the run is waiting on — rolling the table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next — and carries the step's own words.
- **Press** does the one thing you pick in its settings: a move the pack offers, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer.
- **Undo** takes back the last result, and says underneath what it would take back.
- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps.

On a Stream Deck +, Do the next thing and Metric sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second.

A press the run has moved past, or one the page has to take, comes back refused: the key says why for three seconds, then goes back to what it was saying.

## Keeping the page awake

Chrome discards tabs it thinks nobody is looking at, and a discarded tab is a run the deck can no longer see. Keep the run in an OBS dock or a browser source, or exempt Runlog from Memory Saver in the browser's settings.

<Note>
  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one — the run's name and its numbers on your keys — is not.
</Note>

# Streaming a run <Plan tier="plus" />

A **widget** is one panel of the run (the scoreboard, the clock, the race leaderboard) on a page of its own that follows the run as it moves. There is no plugin to install; a widget is a web page, and any streaming app with a browser source can show one. New to Runlog on a stream? [A stream run by dice](#guide/stream-why) says what it is for and what to compare it with.

## The widgets

Under **Stream** in the run's Settings, each widget has **Open** and **Copy address**.

- **Scoreboard**: places, points, and marks in a moderated run.
- **Race**: the leaderboard, as each racer's device reports it.
- **Clock**: the unit's stopwatch or timer, large.
- **Step**: the current step, the constraints in play, the latest result.
- **Stats**: the unit, units done, time on the clock where the run keeps one, the score.
- **Trackers**: resources and counters, as bars and boxes.
- **Ticker**: the last few things that happened (dice, results, points, clocks, a tally moving, the unit closing), one line each, newest on top. It hears the table's gestures the moment they happen and reads the rest from the run, so it catches up after being off scene.
- **Everything, stacked**: the panels above in one column, for a single browser source down the side of a scene. It leaves out what the run has nothing for: a scoreboard with nobody on it, trackers in a pack that has none, the race when the run is not in one.

Three more settings travel in the address: a background (clear, so your scene shows through; solid; or none, the words and numbers alone), a theme pinned for the capture, and a size.

## Chat as input

Under **Stream** → **Chat**, **Take asks** makes a key of the run's own and the address a bot posts to. A channel-point redeem, a chat command or a stream deck button then asks the table to take a move the pack offers ("I died", say) or to roll the table that is waiting. The ask lands in an **Asks** panel beside the people, where you press Accept, or, if you have said so, the table takes it as it lands. [Streamer.bot](#guide/streamer-bot) has the redeem field by field; [the stream API](#guide/stream-tools) has the request for a tool of your own.

## Where to go next

1. [The address that works on a stream](#guide/stream-address): copying the address a browser source needs.
2. [OBS Studio and Streamlabs](#guide/obs): the browser source, field by field.
3. [A dock for the controls](#guide/dock), [StreamElements](#guide/streamelements), [Streamer.bot](#guide/streamer-bot), [TikTok Live](#guide/tiktok), [Kick](#guide/kick), or [a tool of your own](#guide/stream-tools).

<Note>
  Where plans are switched on, widgets are part of Plus, like hosting a table. Where they are not, in the preview or a copy you run
  yourself, they are open to everyone.
</Note>

# Runlog for Stream Deck

Runlog is a referee and run log for dice-driven games: it draws the tables, keeps the score and the clocks, and remembers what happened. This plugin puts the run on your keys, so the next press, a move, undo and the run's numbers are under your hand while you play.

## The keys

- **Connect** — opens the connection to your Runlog account, and closes it again.
- **Run** — names the run the deck is on; press to cycle through the runs you have open, or pick one in its settings.
- **Do the next thing** — presses whatever the run is waiting on, in the step's own words.
- **Press** — one move, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer, set in the key's settings.
- **Undo** — takes back the last result.
- **Metric** — one number from the run: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps.

Do the next thing and Metric also sit on a dial on a Stream Deck +.

## What it needs

- The Stream Deck app, 7.1 or later, on macOS 12 or Windows 10 and up.
- A Runlog account, signed in from any key's settings.
- A run synced to that account and open in a browser, a dock or a browser source: the deck presses through the page holding the run.
- Where plans are switched on, Plus to press a run from the deck. Watching one costs nothing.

## Where to read more

The guide's [A Stream Deck at the table](https://runlog.scrthq.com/guide/stream-deck) sets the keys up, page by page. [Runlog](https://runlog.scrthq.com) is the app.

content.content:
name: "Setup Node and run npm ci"
description: "Setup Node and run npm ci"

author: "Nate Ferrell <nate@scrthq.com>"

inputs:
  node-version:
    description: "Node version to use"
    required: false
    default: 22

runs:
  using: "composite"
  steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
      with:
        node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}

    - name: Cache node modules
      id: cache-npm
      uses: actions/cache@v6
      env:
        cache-name: cache-node-modules
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-build-${{ env.cache-name }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-build-${{ env.cache-name }}-
          ${{ runner.os }}-build-
          ${{ runner.os }}-

    - run: npm ci --cache ~/.npm --prefer-offline
      shell: bash
=== env ===
name: CI/CD

# The path a change takes:
#
#   pull request   ->  the app's checks, the hosting's checks, a diff against both environments
#                      (a fork's pull request gets the checks only)
#   merge queue    ->  the checks again, on main with the queued pull requests merged onto it; no diffs
#   merge to main  ->  build the app, deploy dev (the site stack publishes the build), seed the catalog, tag a release
#   release        ->  "Deploy Production" takes it from there
#
# Production is reached only through a published release, so it always carries
# a version and has always already been to dev. One repository, one pipeline:
# the app and its hosting change together and go out together.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: Which part of the version to increment; auto reads the conventional commit titles since the last tag
        required: true
        default: auto
        type: choice
        options: [auto, patch, minor, major]
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
  # The merge queue builds a branch with the queued pull requests merged onto
  # main and asks for the same checks on it, so a pull request that went green
  # on a stale base is tested and diffed again as it will actually land.
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

env:
  NODE_VERSION: 22
  # CloudFront will not accept a certificate issued anywhere else, and one
  # region avoids a cross-region reference for the sake of one certificate.
  AWS_REGION: us-east-1
  GITHUB_ROLE_NAME: GitHubActionRole

toolUseResult.originalFile:
name: PR title

# The pull request's title becomes the squash commit's title on main, and
# that title decides the version and writes the changelog (see
# CONTRIBUTING.md, "Releases"). So the title is checked here, in
# Conventional Commits form: a type, an optional scope, a short lowercase
# description in the imperative, no period.
#
# pull_request_target rather than pull_request, so the check runs with the
# base repository's token on a fork's pull request too; nothing from the
# pull request is checked out or run, only its title is read.
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]
  # The merge queue asks every required check for a verdict on its merge
  # group. There is no title to check there; the group is made of pull
  # requests that already passed.
  merge_group:

permissions:
  pull-requests: read

jobs:
  title:
    name: Conventional title
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' }}
        uses: amannn/action-semantic-pull-request@v6
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        with:
          types: |
            feat
            fix
            perf
            refactor
            docs
            style
            test
            build
            ci
            chore
            revert
          scopes: |
            run
            designer
            library
            marketplace
            profile
            live
            engine
            schema
            cli
            packs
            hosted
            ci
            docs
            deps
            deps-dev
            release
          requireScope: false
          subjectPattern: ^(?![A-Z]).+(?<!\.)$
          subjectPatternError: |
            The description after the type ("{subject}") should start lowercase, read as an
            instruction ("move the clock under the unit name"), and end without a period.
      - if: ${{ github.event_name == 'merge_group' }}
        run: echo "A merge group has no title to check; its pull requests were checked when they were opened."

37	
38	<Note>
39	  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one — the run's name and its numbers on your keys — is
40	  not.
41	</Note>

With `run=` the address finds that run or is refused, and refused is the better of the two. The panel writes it in for you; anyone building an address by hand should too.
docs/stream-api.md:315:An attached tool is a watcher and nothing more: it may read what a watcher reads and it may not press anything, which is why a watch key is enough and a press key is refused here as everywhere else. Effects come from the run. No tool can reach another tool.

docs/stream-api.md:354:Taking one back names it. Taking back a group names the group. Taking back everything in force uses the reserved id, which is what the end of a run sends, since only the tool knows what it is still holding:
docs/stream-api.md:397:| `tool` | The program this was written for, as that program names itself in its `hello`. Anything else listening is sent nothing and told why. Leave it out and the profile is for whatever is attached, which is how a script of your own works with no ceremony. |

docs/stream-api.md:404:| `to` | A seat's name, or `all`, or left out, which is also everyone. Matched against what a tool said it was sitting in front of, ignoring case. A tool that never said hears only what is for everyone. |

# Runlog for Stream Deck

Runlog is a referee and run log for dice-driven games: it draws the tables, keeps the score and the clocks, and remembers what happened. This plugin puts the run on your keys, so the next press, a move, undo and the run's numbers are under your hand while you play.

## The keys

- **Connect** — opens the connection to your Runlog account, and closes it again.
- **Run** — names the run the deck is on; press to cycle through the runs you have open, or pick one in its settings.
- **Do the next thing** — presses whatever the run is waiting on, in the step's own words.
- **Press** — one move, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer, set in the key's settings.
- **Undo** — takes back the last result.
- **Metric** — one number from the run: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps.

Do the next thing and Metric also sit on a dial on a Stream Deck +.

## What it needs

- The Stream Deck app, 7.1 or later, on macOS 12 or Windows 10 and up.
- A Runlog account, signed in from any key's settings.
- A run synced to that account and open in a browser, a dock or a browser source: the deck presses through the page holding the run.
- Where plans are switched on, Plus to press a run from the deck. Watching one costs nothing.

## Where to read more

The guide's [A Stream Deck at the table](https://runlog.scrthq.com/guide/stream-deck) sets the keys up, page by page. [Runlog](https://runlog.scrthq.com) is the app.

content.content:
# A Stream Deck at the table

Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and six actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Do the next thing, Press, Undo, and Metric. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.

## Signing in

Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.

**Sign in** shows a code and a link. Open the link in a browser, type the code, and you are signed in on the deck; the plugin keeps that sign-in in a file of its own, not in the settings the pages read. Signing in is not connecting: press Connect after.

## Connect

**Connect** opens the connection, and pressing it again closes it. Nothing is open until you press it, and a connection holding no run closes itself after thirty minutes — the key then says _Idle · press to connect_. A deck that is following a run stays up however long the stream goes.

Every other key says **Not connected**, with _press Connect_ beneath it, until the connection is open.

## The run the deck is on

The deck presses through the page that holds the run, so it only ever sees a run that is synced to your account and open on a page somewhere: the app in a browser tab, a [dock](#guide/dock), or a browser source. With nothing synced the keys say **Not synced**; with runs synced but none open, **No run open**.

**Run** names the run the deck is following. Press it to cycle through the runs open to you and pin the next one; its settings list the same runs by name. A pin holds: a pinned run that ends says **That run has ended** rather than moving the deck to whichever run went next. Where one run is open and nothing is pinned, the deck follows that one.

## The keys

- **Do the next thing** presses whatever the run is waiting on — rolling the table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next — and carries the step's own words.
- **Press** does the one thing you pick in its settings: a move the pack offers, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer.
- **Undo** takes back the last result, and says underneath what it would take back.
- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps.

On a Stream Deck +, Do the next thing and Metric sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second.

A press the run has moved past, or one the page has to take, comes back refused: the key says why for three seconds, then goes back to what it was saying.

## Keeping the page awake

Chrome discards tabs it thinks nobody is looking at, and a discarded tab is a run the deck can no longer see. Keep the run in an OBS dock or a browser source, or exempt Runlog from Memory Saver in the browser's settings.

<Note>
  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one — the run's name and its numbers on your keys — is
  not.
</Note>
